If they say that they found 2,000,000 cubic yards of loose rock, the question is, did they find that quantity. Is an official or a Government to be bound hand and foot by an estimate made by an engineer as to the probable cost of something 100 feet under the surface? It would cost a huge sum to bore test pits on every cutting in the rock, It would take years to do it and would be simply impracticable. All that engineers can do is to use their very best judgment. In this case they did so. They found that they could tell practically the number of cubic yards of material to be removed. They said: We believe from our observations that there will be so much loose rock and so much solid rook to be excavated. If it turned out that they were wrong in their estimates, is that an evidence of fraud? It is put forward in this report as such, and I am afraid that, before this debate is over, some of my

hon. friends opposite will say-yes, my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro) read to-night from one of the contracts the estimate made of solid rock and the actual quantity of .solid rock, and 1 believe that he has gone home feeling justified that there is a big steal because there turned out to be more solid rock than the engineer estimated. Yet he did not do himself, nor this House, nor the commission, nor the contractor the justice to get at the bottom of the work and find out whether that cut was properly classified or not.
Another very common mode of finding fault with the construction of this railway is to say that the contracts were sublet. I am coming to that in a moment. I would like my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), when he follows me as I presume he will, to tell me how iri the world you would build a railroad in any other way than by subletting the contracts, and how you would go to work to let the construction of that road, 200, 300 Or 400 miles in the wilderness to men who are able to take ten miles and build that amount of the road. Let us forget that we are talking politics; let us forget this Lynch-Staunton, Gutelius report and get down to common sense. This matter has been referred to by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). I only refer to it here by way of illustration. When my hon. friends opposite are called upon to act, they act in exactly the same way as our party has acted, as any business man will act. Wlien it came to letting the Hudson Bay railway, they let it in 150 or 200-mile contracts. Why did they not let it out in ten-mile contracts? When it came to the Welland canal, they let it out in contracts for $1,000,000 to $6,000,000. Why did they not divide that up into smaller contracts so that the small fellow with the steam shovel and perhaps a few horses could go in and do the work? They know that that man could not do the work. They did not let out the Hudson Bay railway in ten-mile cantracts to small men, because they know that the small men have not the finances to carry on the work. They let it out in 'big contracts for the very same reason that the Transcontinental Commission let it out in big contracts; because in doing so they were sure to get men of sufficient financial ability to ensure the construction of the road with no loss to the Government. I wonder if my friends opposite were ever on railway construction work?
I wonder if they know anything about the work connected with the construction of a 
railway? Do they realize that the main contractor-we will say M. P. Davis, 'because he seems to be the bete noir of my friends opposite when he takes the contract for the construction of 100 miles of railway in a wilderness section of Quebec or Ontario, has to finance the undertaking from start to finish? Do they realize that when he lets the work to a sub-contractor he has to stand 'behind him financially? Do they realize that he is the man who has to advance the money to that sub-contractor with which to buy horses, wagons, ploughs, picks and shovels? Do they realize that the main contractor has to take the responsibility for the wages that are paid? Do they realize that if the sub-contractor goes broke as he has done many times-the main contractor is the man who has to stand behind him? Do they realize that horses die and are killed in the course of the work? Do they realize that it takes possibly $100,000 of machinery to carry out a fifteen or twenty mile contract? Do they realize that that machinery depreciates in value at least 20 per cent in one year? Who is going to furnish this $100,000 of machinery? Your small contractor cannot do it. Can a man with half a dozen horses, a few dump carts and a pile of twenty pound rails finance a scheme like this? The 'commissioners appear to think that he could. If these commissioners know anything about railway construction they are crooked; if they do not know anything about railway construction they should never have been put on the job.
I do not know that any other argument is necessary to meet the assertion of the commissioners with regard to sub-contractors.
My hon. friends opposite proceed to say; Oh, the sub-contractors made money; they made profits on the work. With regard to every one of these twenty-one contracts, in order to prejudice the minds of the people of this country and make them believe that the men connected with the work were crooked, they tel] you the prices received by the main contractor and the prices at which he sublet the contract. This they did, forgetting that the main contractor has to advance the money; forgetting that he has to put up the plant; forgetting that he has to supply the horses, the machinery, the bread which the men eat; forgetting that he has to stand all the loss that takes place. Yet they say, figuring the price which the main contractor got and the price at which he sublet the contract, that so much profit is shown and that the contractor put this money in his pocket, never

having lifted a finger to earn it. I can only say again that if they believe that, they are not fit for the job, and if they do not believe it, they are crooked.
What did M. P. Davis do for his $740,000?

My hon. friend cannot
get me away from the subject which I am discussing; he will have an opportunity later of talking as long as he wants to.
Mr. AMES. What did he give the country for his $740,000?

That was an assignment of the main contract. I will tell you what he did, he put up the deposit which my hon. friends opposite say was so large; he left that deposit there until the work was completed, and took the chances of losing it if the work was not completed according to contract.
Was $740,000 not more than double the amount of his deposit?
I do not know, and I do not care.
You should know.

I suppose Mr. Davis
made a dollar on the contract, just as my hon. friend makes a dollar on his shoe business, and does not do anything for it, either. I am finding no fault with my hon. friend because he does not drive the pegs himself; he has his money invested in the business, and 1 think he is entitled to ^ a reasonable profit. My friends opposite will continence to see, I am sure, in what a ridiculous position they are placing themselves in respect of their commissions. By the time we are through with them, they will curse the day they ever thought of Gutelius.
Do not swear.

speechtext: That is a mistake; I want the hon. gentleman to withdraw that assertion.
I will withdraw it, but that is what the newspapers said. At any rate, my hon. friend will not deny that he made a very hurried trip to Ottawa on accouift of Gutelius.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I did not.

Well, I will withdraw
that also, but a good Tory newspaper in my hon. friend's own town must be wrong.
A newspaper that the hon. gentleman owns himself.

My friends opposite are not through with Gutelius by any means.
I can prophesy this much: just as soon as the hon. acting Minister of Railways becomes Minister of Railways and Canals he will be through with Gutelius.
They do not intend to keep him.
The best man we ever had.

My friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who,
I am sorry to say, is not here to-night, has had something to do with Gutelius, and he is not through with him either. There are a lot of Tory politicians in the Maritime provinces who know something about Gutelius, and who wish they were through with him.
As I have said, these two gentlemen have pointed out the profits made by these contractors. I want to give to the House, from my own personal knowledge, two illustrations of the almost dishonesty of these statements.

Why use the word
' almost?'

The matters to which I am about to refer were within the knowledge of Gutelius and Staunton, or if they were not they ought to have been, because they were matters of public notoriety in the province of New, Brunswick, having been threshed out in the courts in the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec. As a matter of fact they referred to these very matters in the report itself, deferring to contract 3, on page 27 of the report, the commissioners give the price which the main contractor received, and the price which the sub-contractors received. They say:
The value of the work done by subcontractors at their rates.. ..	.. $280,766
Amount paid Toronto Construction
Company for their work	 352,291
Profit	 * *	72,145
Percentage of profit, 20 per cent.
On another part of the page they say:
The Toronto Construction Company had four firms of contractors who undertook the grading on this forty-mile stretch, and another firm of sub-contractors for the concrete work. We

are, however, advised by the Toronto Construction Company that their concrete subcontractors failed and they were obliged to finish the work themselves.
I am reading this from the report of the commission, thus showing that the investigators had gone into the thing deep enough to know the whole story. The facts are that the concrete man fell down on his work-that is just one of those things to which I have been referring. The contractor falls down on his work and the loss is sustained by the main contractor. In this case a man named Ferguson was sub-contractor. He went wrong. I am not going into the details, but in the end the main contractors were obliged to pay him $10,000 to get rid of him. That this amount was a total loss to the main contractors was sworn to in court both in the	province of New Brunswick, and in the city of Hull, Quebec. Then they were compelled to fight two lawsuits on account of this sub-contractor. One was a case tried in the constituency of my hon. friend from Victoria and Madawaska. As usually happens in cases of that kind, the verdict went against the corporation and the Supreme Court set it aside. Another suit was by an Italian, against this construction company and that was fought out in Hull. As usual the verdict went against the corporation. It was taken to the Court of Review, argued twice in Montreal and finally decided in favour of the company. I want to tell my hon. friend that to my own knowledge these two lawsuits cost this company $6,000 to $7,000. There is a ease where $16,000 or $17,000 was absolutely lost, and instead of that company making a profit of $72,000 that meant that they lost $16,000 of that profit. This is a small matter, but it takes off a pretty big slice from the $72,000. These are matters about which Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton should have known and I believe did know and yet they did not hesitate to publish to the House and to the country that this company made $72,000 out of the contract.	-
What is the total value of the contract?

$350,000. Another illustration is on contract 5. I have explained to the House the arrangement made between the commission and the different contractors that they would have a right to put in what they called rock borrow at $1.10J per yard. What I am saying is a matter of co .ion knowledge, not fMr. Carvell.]
only amongst contractors on the Transcontinental in New Brunswick, but among many other people as well. You will find at page 29 of the report the particulars of this contract No. 5. This was the big contract, the contract in which occurred the big viaduct, the contract which cost most per mile of any on the whole road. The commissioners give here the main contractor's price and the sub-contractors' prices, as in every other case, and figure out that the main contractors made I think something like $699,000 profit. But that was on a big work amounting to $2,518,000. They say this was a profit of 27J per cent. One of the sub-contractors of the main contractors were two young men, sons of one of the principal stockholders in the main company. And these two young men took the contract for this rock borrow, for which the Government paid $1.10J per yard, at the ridiculous rate of 75 cents per yard. I do not know why it was done, but it was done anyway, and you will find at page 30 the report of this sub-contract; solid rock borrow, main contractors, $1.10J, sub-contractors, 75 cents. It was necessary to have one of these big fills put in as early as possible in order to get the steel to the big viaduct. The result was that these sub-contractors worked day and night and summer and winter for a year and a half to get it through and lost about $50,000 on the transaction. The sub-contractors did not have that much money, or	anything like	it. The	result
was that the $50,000 came out of the main contractor-and Mr. Gutelius knows it, or ought to know it. There i? nc+ a contractor on the Grand Trunk i'ac fic in New Brunswick but knows it, hardly a business man but knows it. They knew that the main contractor lost about $50,000 on th's roc!: borrow and this $50,000 should have come off the profit; but Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Staunton do not say that, they do not hesitate to tell the House and the country that these men have made all this profit. I venture to say that if you went from Moncton to Winnipeg and could find out the inside history of all these contracts you would not find a contract on the whole road that was free from such things as this
Why did the main contractors have to pay that $50,000? Were they legally bound or was it just because of the relationship between them?

They had to pay it. Does not my hon. friend know that they had to pay for the wages and the supplies? These

20fi9
young men did not have any steam shovels or any heavy plant. They had to buy three steam shovels and a lot of donkey engines and track equipment, as well as furnishing probably thirty of forty horses. They had to spend $100,000 on plant to carry out the work. These young men did not have the money, they were like the rest of the subcontractors ; and the main contractors advanced the money with which to buy the plant.
They loaned it.

All right, they advanced it anyway, they paid the money out. Then they had to pay the wages every month and whatever the expenses were and when they came to settle the matter up in the end they found they were $50,000 out of pocket. That i3 the way it works out, that is what I have been trying to explain and I do not believe that there is any contract on the road in which you will not find that something has happened exactly as I have described in reference to contract No. 5.
Is there anything in the evidence about the $50,000?

No, I am saying that it is well known to every contractor in the Maritime provinces. It is something about which my hon. friends can satisfy themselves, the commission can give them the information. The chief engineer knows all about it, he has been over the work again and again. Mr. Woods, the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, knows all about it. They all know all about it and I believe that Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Staunton knew all about it, but they took mighty good pains not to say anything about it.
I have given you three illustrations taken from these contracts in New Brunswick that I know all -about myself, and I have pointed out the manner in which these gentlemen have, in my judgment, absolutely suppressed the evidence necessary to give the real facts of the case. Do you wionder that the hon. member for South Renfrew told you that he did not believe the Government believed in the truth of this report, and do you wonder that we attack it and ask this House to pass an amendment to the motion to go into Supply, condemning the Government for asking the country -and this House to accept such a report?
We (have heard a good deal about the question of overbreak and improper classification. I have described the classification. I am going back now to another
phase of it. My friends -say that there was practically collusion existing between the commission and its engineers and the contractors by which the contractors were allowed to take out much larger quantities of solid rock than were necess-ary because they were getting a big price for it and making money out of it. Witness after witness was examined as to how much overbreaks ought to be taken out. One man said from 25 to 30 per cent. -I think the commission find as a fact that a man ought not to be fined if he takes out 20 per cent more than the actual prism measine-ment of the cut. My friend the acting Minister of Railways will understand that if you put in -a blast of explosives -and you have a rock face of 10, 20, 30 or 40 feet high, you have to take that out wide enough and deep enough to meet your prism measurement, you cannot hew that as you would with ,a chisel. You have to put in enough explosives to take it out, because if you leave what is call-ed a toe at the foot it will cost-you three or four times as much to take that out as it is worth.
In every case they took out more than the actual -amount required. As I stated before, the commission found that twenty per cent would not be an unreasonable amount, but evidence was given by engineers to the effect that twenty-five per cent or thirty per cent would not be unreasonable. In contract ' F ' it was admitted that they took out more than twenty-fivie per cent in many cases. The engineers said they wanted the material to fill up holes and the chief engineer said:	You must get out so. much
every month. And they took it out and filled up the holes and very little material was wasted. Trouble arose about this overbreak. They said it was unfair classification and therefore something which should be condemned. We threshed this out in the House time and again between 1907 and 1910, and in the end it became so serious that a board of arbitration was appointed and sent out to make a report. My hon. friend from Renfrew has already referred to that. I need only say that under the National Transcontinental Act, in case the engineers could not agree upon any question of this kind, it was to be referred for final decision to a board of arbitrators composed of the chief engineer of the commission, the Grand Trunk Pacific engineer and a third man to be appointed by them, if they could agree. If they could not agree, the third man was to be appointed by the Chief Justice of Canada. They failed to

agree and the Chief Justice appointed Mr. Collingwood Schreiber. They went out on the work and finally found that about
525.000	yards of overbreak was taken out more than should have been. They said the contractor must not receive pay for that
500.000	yards. Messrs. Staunton and Gute-lius report that the amount should have been a little over 700,000 yards, but my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways knows that since this Government came into power they have settled with that contractor not for 500,000 yards, not for 700,000 yards but for a sum not much more than half the cost of the 500,000 yards.
I do not know anything about that.
Who was the contractor?
J. D. McArthur.
When	did they settle?

Since	this Government
came into power. They have paid that man probably a quarter of a million dollars more than the arbitrators said he should have got.

I think the minister
should know that.

It is another proof that they do not believe the Staunton-Gutelius report. They know it is not a fair report. Either it is a fair report or it is crooked, one or the other; if it is straight, the Government is crooked, and they can take which horn of the dilemma they like.

They are both
crooked.

I am not making any assertions. I am only giving the arguments and my hon. friend the acting Minister of. Railways can make the application. The more we delve into this thing the more we feel that the minister, at least, realizes he has made a mistake. They were so anxious for political capital against their opponents that they chose two men not one-quarter big enough for the job, who simply went at it blind and reported everything that came into their small minds in order to hurt their opponents. Now the whole thing is acting as a boomerang against the men who have to father the report. And that report is to be sent broadcast all over the country. I am told that they are printing a quarter of a millions copies, so that one may be put in the hands of each elector, to make a little political capital for themselves. But I hope that my hon. friend, now that we have [Mr. Carvell.j
pointed out the iniquities of the report, will cancel the order and leave well enough alone, or bad enough alone.
The people will cancel the Government.

I would like to ask the hon. member a question. Did it ever strike him as strange that there was no trouble about overbreak on the line between Graham and Port Arthur where the Grand Trunk Pacific used wooden trestles?

I do not know anything about it. We are not investigating that part of the line. The Government of this country did not build that portion, but the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend may know. He has been over the line, but I have not. I do not see the application. If my hon. friend will point out to me any section of the National Transcontinental railway on which that occurred, I will try to answer him. I do not think he can.
If you wish me to make my point clear I will do so.

I understand the point of my hon. friend. He says that there were wooden trestles on the Grand Trunk Pacific line from Graham to Port Arthur and no overbreak on that road. I do not know anything about that. The Government of this country had nothing to do with it. My non. friend might as well say there was no overbreak on the Canadian Pacific railway through the Rockies.
The hon. member recognizes the significance of my question.
Has the hon. mem-bef seen the classification on that road?
That is not the point. The point I wish to bring to the .attention of the House is this: wherever there was not a demand for an unnecessary fill, there was not a corresponding increase in overbreak.

Is my hon. friend such a simpleton as not to know that these holes have to be filled up some time? If the Grand Trunk Pacific chooses to fill these trestles two or five years from now, or the Government chooses to fill them as construction proceeds, where is the difference?
I do not know what my hon. friend is driving at.

There is a great difference
in the price of material used.

I want to ask my hon.
friend a question. Will he tell me why this Government has not obeyed the findings of their arbitrators, and why they have allowed McArthur a quarter of a million dollars more than he ought to have got according to the findings of the commission?
You will have to ask somebody else.
When my hon. friend is asked a question germane to the issue he gets behind anything, rather than give a straight answer. He knows the trouble.

out, after everything had dried up, after the rain had broken up the small pieces, and after the surface had all been smoothed down and the grass had grown up. There was an entirely different condition of affairs. The net result of Mr. Goodwin's and Mr. Gutelius' efforts with reference to contract No. 1, a contract involving $2,000,000, was that they reported that about $45,000 should be taken off this whole amount after it had been settled by Ithe Board of Arbitration. That was a Grand Trunk Pacific contract, too. Then they came next to contract No. 2, but they did not touch that at all. Contracts Nos. 3 and 4 were sub-let to the Toronto Construction Company, and they took abouit the same amount from them. Then they came to the Kitchen contract- contract No. 5-and they took about $35,000 from him.
Either these men were right or they were wrong in taking from the contractors this amount of money, either they were honest or dishonest, either they were ignorant or they were knowing-I do not know which they were, and my hon. friends can take whichever hom of the dilemma they choose. If Gutelius and Goodwin were right in taking that $35,000 from the Kitchen contract, they should have taken it off and kept it off.	If they were
right in taking $35,000 from the Corbett contract, they should have taken it off and kept it off. But they were up against men who knew as much as they did, and both Corbett and Kitchen said: We will not allow this thing to take place; we will fighit you. Having got up against two men who had a good deal of sand and a little money besides, they said to them: Come, let us reason together, let us see if we cannot compromise this matter; we say that the commission should take this money off, but we do not want to take it off; let us get' together. The result was that they allowed on No. 1 contract about $18,000, and on No. 5 about $15,000. I want to know if these men are big enough for their jobs. If these men were right in taking off that money, were they right in making the compromise and in paying money wthich they ought not to have paid? Remember, they had the money in their own hands. At that time they had probably $100,000 of Mr. Kitchen's money in their own hands, probably more. Although they had that amount of money in their hands, did they keep it out? No, Sir, they [Mr. Carvell. 1
did not keep it out. They quibbled, but when they found they were up against a lawsuit they backed down.
M.r. AMES: Had the contractors the engineer's certificate?
The contractors had the ordinary progress estimates.
Signed by the engineers?

Certainly, they got them month by month. But my hon. friend cannot get behind that. If my hon. friend will read the contract he will find that everything is put up to the final decision of the chief engineer. No matter what the progress estimates say, it is the chief engineer who decides, and if they cannot agree with the chief engineer, then it is submitted to arbitration. It only comes back to this again that these men, in order to find fault with the former commissioners, in order to prove that there was something crooked, started in to do that which they did not have the manhood to stand up to and see through to the end. Then they said that they could take $35,000 off these contracts, but they did not have the sand to stand by that declaration, and when they found themselves face to face with a lawsuit, and when they found themselves up against the judgment of bigger men than themselves, they backed down, just as you would expect men of that class to do, and - they said: Lei us settle this. These contractors, rather than have a lawsuit over a paltry sum of $15,000 in a contract involving $2,000,000, accepted the settlement. They will go before the country and they will say: look at these crooked engineers, they allowed Kitchen $15,000 more than they ought to have allowed him, and we will make him give restitution. That is an illustration of what has been going on, ever since these gentlemen took possession of this road in 1911.

Are these district engineers
still in the employ of the Transcontinental Commission?	.

Some of them are. Mr. Foss was kept in their employ until the month of January last and then he was told that they had no further use for him.
I do not know why they kept him; he had nothing to do and they paid him a big fat *salary for doing it. I am glad they did, .however, because he is a man for whom I have the highest esteem. There was no-

body more surprised than Mr. Foss at being kept on, but I presume they kept him on for some purposes. There are some lawsuits that are not settled yet, and perhaps they kept him on to have a string on Mr. Foss, but if they did they did not know their man, and when the lawsuits come on, a.: probably they will, you will hear of Mr. Foss and have his opinion put up against that of Mr. Gutelius.
I am sorry the Minister of Marine is not here, because I have a few things I would like to say in his presence, and I am also sorry the Prime Minister is not in the House. As an eastern man, if there is one statement in this most remarkable document to which I take more violent exception than to another, it is the concluding paragraph of the report, at page 138, which reads:
This commission does not think that the National Transcontinental railway should have been constructed east of Lfivis, which was done at a cost of $35,000,000, first,-because the Government at that time had a railway in operation between L6vis and Moncton, the Intercolonial; second,-because the National Transcontinental railway would only be thirty-three miles shorter ; third,-because the gradients on the National Transcontinental railway are greater than those on the Intercolonial railway ; and fourth,-because the grades on the Intercolonial railway can be reduced to four-tenths per cent, east-bound and six-tenths per cent westbound, whereas it is practically impossible according to the construction of the National Transcontinental railway, to reduce the 1.10 per cent grade at 146 miles west of Moncton and the 1.10 per cent grade at lake Polienagamook.
There are two reasons why I violently dissent from the conclusion found in that statement. In the first place, while it may not be a false conclusion, it is an unfair conclusion from the facts. They attempt to leave the impression that the general grades, on that portion of the road east of Levis, are greater than they are on the Intercolonial. These gentlemen know better than that, but they also know there are thousands of people in the country who will he deceived by the false statement they are making. It is a fact that there are two points on the road, between Levis and Moncton, on which there is a grade of 1-1. The reason for that is, that they figured out that two engines will draw the same load on a 1-1 grade that one engine will on a 0-4 grade. Therefore, in two cases where the cost of making the 0-4 road would be exceedingly excessive, they resort to what is called a pusher grade. In one case, it is something like ten or eleven miles long, and in the other case it is thirteen miles long, and these grades are on different divisions. This means that for
heavy traffic they would simply have to keep an extra engine at the foot of these . grades. On the 500 miles between Quebec and Moncton there are only two spots where they have exceeded the ruling grade of 0.4 east and 0.6 west. But if the present Government introduced these grades everywhere, then you would have to keep an engine everywhere there was such a grade, and you would be reducing the hauling capacity of the road to a one per cent road. That is a thing that these commissioners did not report to the public, but they tried to leave the impression that this road is practically a one per cent road. They know better than that.
These gentlemen find a great deal of fault with the construction of the Little Salmon river viaduct. I know that my friend from St. Antoine will say that Mr. Foss advocated the construction of pusher grades at the Little Salmon river viaduct, and I admit that. But if that had been done, the character of the road would have been degraded. The hon. member will have to know something about the history of the location of this road in the province of New Brunswick to understand the real reason why this report was made. It was made for the purpose of eliminating expense, and Mr. Foss stated that probably one and a half million dollars or a little more could have been saved by putting in a pusher grade across the Salmon river, a few feet above the water level, rather than building a viaduct. But if that were done you would be getting back to what the Intercolonial is; you would be degrading the whole road. If you put in that kind of grade at Coal creek and Chipman crossing, you would have the same condition of affairs. It is purely a question of policy whether the Government should have adhered to the 0.4 road or not. I do not have to call on the evidence of engineers to tell me that you can haul more freight and haul it cheaper over a level road than you can over a
12 m. hilly road. Neither do I have to be told that on a velocity grade, if you strike a slippery rail, or if your engine is not steaming properly, you are stalled, and there is nothing to do when you are stalled but cut your train in two; haul over the hill what cars you can, and then come back for the rest, losing several hours and eating up all the profit you get for carrying that freight. Any man who ever drove an automobile knows what you can do and what you cannot do on a velocity grade. He knows that you start down a hill on one side, and sometimes you

will get over the opposite hill, if everything is all right, but sometimes your carbureter is out of order and you will get stalled.
Or it is a question whether your gasoline is as good as the last tankful was. It is a question of a hundred different things. The same question that applies to a man driving an automobile over a velocity grade applie to an engineer who is trying to haul freight over a velocity grade. While I am not an engineer, I profess to have some common sense. So far as I am concerned, if there is anything for which I give the old commission credit it is for the fact that they were willing to accept the opinions of the best engineers in the world; that they wanted to build a road that would carry the grain from the West to the seaboard and carry back the manufactured articles.
There is one thing that my hon. friends have failed to recognize in all this transaction. We were not doing as the former Conservative Government did, when they subsidized the Canadian Pacific railway. I am not finding any fault with the Government for the assistance they gave to the Canadian Pacific railway. I have a wonderful admiration for the Canadian Pacific railway except at election time. I am a very good friend of the Canadian Pacific railway and they are very good friends of mine except at election time. When an election comes on, they absolutely put out of my constituency every man who they think will vote for me.
And send him up to my constituency

Yes. As a railway corporation they have done a wonderful work in developing and opening up Canada. The old Conservative Government gave them $25,000,000, some million dollars of completed road and land which is worth at least $300,000,000 to them. They exempted them from taxation; they gave them a subsidy on pretty nearly every mile of road they own in Canada. The Conservative party have assisted them in every form from the beginning of the road down to the present day and they are still assisting them. They are assisting Mackenzie and Mann; they gave them $17,000,000 last year and are going to give them $50,000,000 this year.
Not on your life.

My hon. friend from
Calgary is not here, so I am safe in making this statement. Remember that every dollar of money, every acre of land, every
I Mr. Carvell.l
exemption from taxation, everything which they have given to the Canadian Northern railway or the Canadian Pacific railway, they have given to those railways. It has gone from the people of Canada. We have no string upon it; we shall never get it back; we do not expect to get it back; it is theirs and theirs absolutely. Every dollar we are putting into the National Transcontinental railway is our own money, no matter whether it be $161,000,000, or whether you add compound interest for the next fifty years and make it $300,000,000 or $400,000,000 by simply compounding the interest long enough, no matter how much the road may have cost in the gross or per mile, no matter whether we have absolutely solid fill instead of wooden trestles, no matter whether we have steel bridges instead of wooden ones, no matter whether we have 0.4 per cent grades on which we can haul 2,000 or 2,500 tons per train as compared with 800 or 900 tons on the best road in Canada outside of the National Transcontinental railway, no matter what conditions may exist the Nation Transcontinental railway belongs to the people of Canada. We are leasing the railway to a company which will pay us three per cent for forty-three years, and at the end of that period every dollar put into that road, every dollar of improvement upon it, every bit of improvement that has taken place in the country along the location of the road, everything that has gone into that road will come back absolutely to the people of Canada, exactly as we gave it to the railway only made more valuable by the improvements, by the opening up of the country and by the business developed. In my judgment it is one of the finest assets which the Dominion of Canada possesses to-day. If I had not enough faith in the future of this great country to justify the building of a road like that, when it is our own road and will come back to us, I would consider myself a pretty small Canadian and not fit to occupy a seat in this Parliament or in any other parliament in Canada. When my hon. friends come to discuss this question I hope they will not fail to realize the difference between the fact that, as far as other railway companies are concerned, we are giving money away by tens and hundreds of millions of dollars, whereas in this case we are putting the money into our own road; we are going to receive interest on it for forty-three years and then the road will come back to us and will be the property of Canada and of every man who lives in Canada. There is every difference in the world between the two

cases. What is the use of handing over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to operate a road built of wooden trestles, with velocity grades on which you cannot do business. What is the'use of it when it comes back to us? If they fill these trestles later on, we shall have to pay for the work. My hon. friends do not imagine for a moment that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are going to fill these trestles. My hon. friends say: Oh, but we could have filled these trestles more cheaply than you did. They try to prove that by saying that the Grand Trunk Pacific railway said: We will fill these trestles for 25 cents a yard. Do they realize that probably 50 cents a yard was the average cost of filling up these holes? It is in the evidence; it is a well known fact, something that Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton took great pains to keep in the back ground, that it has cost practically 25 cents a yard to build those trestles. When those trestles have been built, you will have to cover them up. You cannot take them out and use them over again. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company said: After the trestles are built for us, we will haul material and put it down there for 25 cents a yard. They could afford to do so but they would not build the trestles in addition to that. The ordinary contractor does not build standard trestles as a rule; he builds temporary trestles. The great majority of these fills were made with pony equipment, donkey engines as they are called. The contractors run out a trestle; they fill up a grade probably ten, fifteen or twenty feet; then they raise the grade and put another temporary trestle on top of that. It probably does not cost them more than three or four cents a yard for temporary trestles, whereas if they had to build standard trestles it would cost them 25 cents and the cost of filling them in afterwards. How much would the people of this country have saved if wooden trestles had been built instead of standard ones?
Very little, if anything.

The commissioners take care to say, in regard to every one of these contracts, that the contractors make so much money on this and so much on that. In every case they say that the contractors made money on their train-hauled material. I believe that the contractors made more money on the train-hauled material than they ever expected to make, and I believe that there is perhaps no item in the specification that was so profitable to the
contractors as was the train-hauled material, and why? When these gentlemen were called upon to tender, they only tendered for a price for train-hauled material per yard. These prices all averaged around forty or forty-three cents. They were basing their price upon their previous experience, and they had been building railroads of one per cent grades; they had never built a four-tenths road. When they got down to a four-tenths road they found that they were able to haul their material for a great deal less money than they could on a one per cent road. I do believe they made money on it; I will give my friends an illustration. In New Brunswick a firm of sub-contractors engaged on contract 6 had a splendid standard outfit, and could haul twenty to twenty-one cars of gravel to the trainload. 'That same firm are building a Gutelius road in my county at the present time-one of those tramways with seven and eight degree curves and over one per cent grades. It is costing the province of New Brunswick a nice penny to build it too. The province of New Brunswick has guaranteed the bonds for $25,000 a mile; it is one of those Tory political roads. Now they are coming back to the provincial legislature for an additional guarantee of bonds to the extent of $10,000 a mile, and I suppose they will get it.
Where is the money going?

It is going into the hands of a Yankee by the name of Gould. I wish my friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries were here, because he is particularly interested in that line. In addition they get from this Government a subsidy of $6,400 a mile.
Is it let to sub-contractors?
Every yard of it. The contractor has not a shovel, a cart-even a horse. He has nothing there but an automobile.
Send Gutelius after him.

Gutelius knows all about him; Gutelius is one of his particular chums. They are building one of Gutelius's favourite roads-the same contractors, with the same engines, the same shovels, the same outfit, and they are able to haul at the very best seven cars of material, and sometimes only six, to the train. This illustrates the difference between a four-tenths road and a one per cent road.
Is it a surface road?

It is practically a surface road. There is no doubt of the fact that they are making a lot of money out of it. However, I am pointing that out merely to show the results of operations so far as the two different kinds of roads are concerned; when these contractors get on a four-tenths road I do believe they make money on their train-hauled material. Do you mean to tell me that if a man tenders for a contract against the whole world-and in every case the low man gets the contract-it being found later that he is going to make money on a certain portion of his contract, the Government should say to him: We made a mistake; you are going to make money on that particular part of your work; we will take that from you and you can finish the part of the work on which there is no profit? It is all very well for Gutelius to preach that principle, but no man knows better than he that that does not work out in actual practice. This is but another evidence of the utter nonsense of the whole report.
There is another reason why I object to the last clause of this report even more strongly than to the other misstatements it contains about the character of the road. If there is any portion of this Dominion which did not make any too good a bargain when it came into Confederation, it is the Maritime provinces. I do not say that these provinces would like to withdraw from Confederation; we are in, and perhaps it is best for us to stay in, but up to the present time it has been a losing game. We have had no opportunity of selling our produce to the rest of Canada; we have had to find a market for our produce, with the exception of coal, and, perhaps, potatoes, wherever we could. On account of transportation and tariff conditions, we have been compelled to buy our machinery, flour, clothing and, to a considerable extent, our manufactured articles, from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It has been a long, hard and up-hill fight. If the Maritime provinces have not increased in population as rapidly as the other provinces of Canada have, it is because of the economic conditions against which we have been fighting. We have paid our proportion of the $100,000,000 which has gone into the construction of canals, and we fire getting not a dollar in return for it. We are paying our share of all the millions of dollars that have gone into great public works-millions of dollars in the harbour

of Montreal, millions in the harbour of Quebec, millions in Toronto, millions in Vancouver, millions in Victoria, millions all through this .country.

Millions in Halifax,
millions in St. John.

Very few. We are coming to our own at the present time, but we started only four or five years ago to do it- no thanks to this Government. We have paid our shares, and we have paid it willingly. Any man from the Maritime provinces who will vote to sustain this report is a traitor to this country and has not the best interests of his province at heart. I will watch this vote with interest. I want to see what attitude my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will take on this question; I want to see what attitude every other member from the Maritime provinces will take in the matter. It is said that we should pay our share of the $150,000,000 for building a railway from Winnipeg to Quebec, though the Maritime provinces have no rights of extension in the eastern provinces, no right to obtain the benefit of cheap transportation from west to east or to build up their ports. Do my hon. friends tell me it is reasonable to expect the Maritime provinces to accept a situation like that? Are my friends the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries going to vote for a proposition of that kind? If for no other reason than the nature of the conclusion of this report, I would feel that every man from the Maritime provinces, no matter on which side of Mr. Speaker he sits, is in honour bound to condemn this report not only by his word but by his vote and by every means in his power. It should be condemned if for no other reason than because of the gratuitous insult it offers to the people of the Maritime provinces in its concluding words. In the first place the matter to which it refers is a question of policy which was settled by the people of this country in two elections: it does not concern these commissioners at all. The report offers a gratuitous insult which I do not believe the Prime Minister knew was in the document or he would not have allowed it to be circulated in its present form. It is there, however, and the Prime Minister must take the responsibility.

The acting Minister of
Railways approved the report.

I was not here and I did not hear his remarks. I must confess that I had a better opinion of him.

I think I may be pardoned if for a few moments I refer to a matter connected with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway which is not dealt with in this report. In the province of New Brunswick the people were led to believe that the city of St. John would be one of the terminals of the road. The late Government when in power had made arrangements to build the road of which I have been speaking, the Valley railway, which was to be the connection between the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the city of St. John. My hon. friends the enemy have possession of things down there now; they are building a tramway, which I have described, which does not go within 25 miles of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. It does not go to St. John, and they never intend that it shall go there.
It starts from the Canadian Pacific railway at Andover, and it is going to end on the -Canadian Pacific railway at Westfield, at least that is my prophecy, and it will only be a matter of a week or so now until we see if my prophecy is correct. Years have gone by, and not a finger has been lifted to give St. John access to this great work. We are paying our share and getting no benefit, and as far as I can see years more will go by and we will not have any chance of participating in the benefits I wish that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) were here to-night.
I hope that before the debate concludes he will take the people of New Brunswick into his confidence and tell them what he is doing and what ihe hopes to do in order to give his own city connection with this work, and put'the people of that city in a position to receive their portion of the benefits which they have fondly hoped they would receive from the expenditure of millions on this great project. He is not here; I am afraid he will be as mum on this question as he was during the debate in this House on the famous Gutelius agreement by which our rightful freight business is carried by Mr. Gutelius, for one-half what it -actually costs to transport it, away to Halifax. The hon. minister was very anxious to have a chance to talk about it, so anxious that he got the Minister of Public Works to adjourn the debate in order that he might discuss it later on. The resolution went to the bone pile and is there yet, it has never been called up and never will be. The minister has not had an opportunity to discuss it, he never will, and I am afraid he will be quite as silent in this debate as 132)	REVISED
he has been on all other matters referring to his own -city, his own constituency, and our great commercial port. These things are not in the report, but they are of great importance to all the electors of New Brunswick, and of more special importance to the electors of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries than all of us put together.
I have discussed this report at greater length than I intended. It is a rather fascinating subject; a man might speak for three or four hours to-day and go on for three or four hours more to-morrow because, Sir, it is, in my judgment, so unfair, so full of unfair statements, so unfair to the Liberal party, so unfair to the former commissioners, so unfair to Canada as a whole, that a man hardly has parliamentary language in which to describe his real feelings, not only towards the report but towards the men who are responsible for it-and when I use that expression I do not mean simply the two tools, Gutelius and Staunton, but I mean the whole Government that stands behind it. I hope that before the debate concludes the acting Minister of Railways will be convinced, as he must in fact now be convinced, that it is a partisan report, founded upon false premises, founded upon lack of evidence, a report not justified by the evidence, a report not in the interests of the country, and that he will see that the Government will either accept the amendment of the hon. member for South Renfrew or formally state in the House that they do not father the report, do not stand by it-because we know by their conduct that they are not standing by it-and that they will by their words say to the people of Canada, as they have been doing for months by their actions in allowing moneys which these men say should not be allowed and doing a hundred things which these men condemn, that they do not endorse the report. I have tried to present this matter exactly as I feel about it, not only from the standpoint of my native province but of Canada as a whole. As the hon. member for South Renfrew said, this is not a question involving New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, but a question involving the good name, the honesty, the business reputation and the financial standing of the whole of Canada. That report is one which I believe has done more to injure our fair name in the markets of the world than anything that has happened in our lifetime and is something which I hope never will be repeated. I certainly hope it will never be repeated merely for party purposes, for that has been the whole object and aim of this nefarious report.
